## Verdict: do not publish as written

Both sentences carry distinct, separately actionable problems under German law. HWG applies to medical devices (§ 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG references MDR Art. 2 Nr. 1), and this is advertising outside professional circles ("außerhalb der Fachkreise"), which triggers the § 11 content bans.

### Sentence 1 — "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist"

**§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 2 HWG — high confidence, high severity.** Public-facing advertising may not state that a product is "ärztlich … oder anderweitig fachlich empfohlen oder geprüft." A named cardiologist's recommendation is the textbook case. There is no substantiation defence here — the ban is on the *form* of the claim, not its truth. Even a genuinely held, unpaid, accurate endorsement is prohibited.

Secondary exposure on the same line:
- **§ 5a UWG** if the relationship is compensated and undisclosed.
- **§ 5 UWG / § 3 HWG** if "Professor" or "cardiologist" isn't precisely accurate — the German specialty designation is *Facharzt für Innere Medizin und Kardiologie*, and academic titles are protected.
- **§ 27 MBO-Ä** — the physician is separately barred from lending their name to commercial product advertising. This is your partner's risk, but it becomes your problem when the Ärztekammer contacts them.
- If the page pairs this with an image of him in a white coat or examining a patient, that's an additional hit under **§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 4 HWG**.

**Fix:** remove it. The endorsement can live behind an HCP-gated section, since § 11 only restricts advertising outside professional circles — but the brief says no gating, so it's out.

### Sentence 2 — "Don't gamble with your heart — check your pressure daily"

**§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 7 HWG — high confidence, high severity.** Bans copy "geeignet, Angstgefühle hervorzurufen oder auszunutzen." "Spielen Sie nicht mit Ihrem Herzen" is a fear appeal built on implied cardiac catastrophe, aimed at an ungated general audience. This is the clearest kind of Nr. 7 case.

**§ 3 HWG / MDR Art. 7 — high severity.** The two clauses combine into an implied claim that daily use of the monitor protects your heart. The device measures blood pressure; it does not reduce cardiovascular risk. That's a therapeutic effect the product does not have (§ 3 Nr. 1 HWG) and a false impression as to properties (MDR Art. 7(b)).

**"Daily" — medium severity, needs a document check.** Check this against your intended purpose and IFU. ESH/Hochdruckliga guidance frames home monitoring as structured 7-day schedules around clinical review, morning and evening, not indefinite daily measurement by the general population. If your intended purpose says frequency is per healthcare-professional advice, "check your pressure daily" is a use beyond the assessed intended purpose (MDR Art. 7(d)) as well as unsolicited clinical advice.

**Missing risk/limitation statement — MDR Art. 7(c).** The copy positions self-measurement as the safeguard with no indication that it doesn't replace medical assessment.

### Enforcement reality

In Germany the practical threat isn't BfArM — it's **§ 3a UWG**. An HWG breach is a per-se unfair-competition violation, and Wettbewerbszentrale, the Verband Sozialer Wettbewerb, and competitors actively police exactly this pattern. Expect an Abmahnung with Unterlassungserklärung and cost claim, not a warning letter.

### Suggested replacement

```
Blutdruck zuhause zuverlässig messen.
Klinisch validierte Messgenauigkeit nach ISO 81060-2.
Regelmäßige Selbstmessung hilft Ihnen und Ihrer Ärztin oder
Ihrem Arzt, Ihre Werte im Blick zu behalten.
Messhäufigkeit nach ärztlicher Empfehlung.
Die Selbstmessung ersetzt keine ärztliche Diagnose.
```

This swaps borrowed personal authority for verifiable product fact, drops the fear frame, and keeps frequency guidance where it belongs.

### One gray zone to take to counsel

If you want an authority signal to replace the professor, note that Nr. 2 bans "empfohlen **oder geprüft**" — so a "fachlich geprüft" test seal is not automatically safe either. The Deutsche Hochdruckliga Prüfsiegel is widely used on German BP monitors, and the arguable position is that a neutral factual reference to a technical standard is product-characteristic information rather than a professional endorsement. That argument is contested. The safer framing is the one above: state validation as a measurement-accuracy fact tied to the standard, not as a seal of approval.

### Open questions for you

1. Does the intended purpose in your technical documentation support daily self-measurement by unsupervised consumers?
2. Is the device clinically validated to ISO 81060-2? If not, drop that line — I've assumed it is.
3. Is "Professor Schmidt" a real, correctly-titled cardiologist, and is the arrangement compensated? Relevant to the residual UWG exposure if any version of the endorsement survives elsewhere.

I've assessed this against HWG, MDR Art. 7, and UWG as they stand; the paragraph numbering is worth a confirmation pass with German regulatory counsel before you rely on it in a response to an Abmahnung.

# Device Claims Review: CGM marketing copy (3 lines, 20 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-09
**Device:** Continuous glucose monitor — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** Publikum — consumer/patient-facing. HWG § 11 (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12) would be in scope for the German market.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **Germany not confirmed** — HWG/UWG findings below are flagged conditional on DE targeting.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 0 substantiate, 0 OK.**

The copy's structure is the problem, not any single word. The intended purpose contains an express carve-out — readings do **not** replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change — and the copy's payoff line does exactly what the carve-out excludes, while nothing anywhere surfaces the limitation. That makes this a limb (d) problem, which evidence cannot cure.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d), and Art. 7(b)
**Why:** (d) — the assessed intended purpose is *monitoring*, with treatment decisions during rapid glucose change expressly excluded. Unqualified "dose with confidence" suggests the device is fit for insulin dosing in **all** conditions, including the excluded ones; that is "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". (b) — it simultaneously creates "a false impression regarding treatment", positioning a monitoring device as a dosing device.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured only by narrowing the claim, or by extending the conformity assessment to cover a dosing indication.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — "Erfolg mit Sicherheit": "with confidence" promises certainty of outcome on precisely the decision the intended purpose says the device cannot carry alone. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — *Zwecktauglichkeit* and *von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse*. Both conditional on the copy running in Germany.
**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** `"Confirm with a fingerstick before dosing when your glucose is changing rapidly."`

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(c)
**Why:** (c) is an omission test. The likely risk here is not inferred from the device category — it is written into the intended purpose itself: reliance on readings for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change. In a diabetes context that risk is hypo- or hyperglycaemia from a mis-dose. Nothing in the asset informs "the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose", and "real-time" actively works against the disclosure by implying no latency.
**Evidence needed:** Measurement interval and reported lag/accuracy figures (lag time, MARD, and performance during rapid rate-of-change) from the technical documentation — to confirm "every 5 minutes" and to check whether "real-time" is defensible as used.
**Call:** **Reword.** I'm not flagging "real-time" as a standalone (a) breach — *rtCGM* is established terminology distinguishing continuous from intermittently-scanned sensors. It's the combination of "real-time" with zero limitation text that makes (c) bite.
**Suggested fix:** `"Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."` — plus the limitation line above. If you keep "real-time", the limitation line becomes mandatory, not optional.

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) — weaker than the two above, but real
**Why:** The assessed purpose is **interstitial** glucose monitoring. To a patient audience, "know your glucose" reads as blood glucose, and the interstitial/blood distinction is the exact reason the carve-out exists. Framing that as settled knowledge "at a glance" contributes to a false impression about what the reading is.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — a wording issue.
**Call:** **Reword.**
**Suggested fix:** `"Know your glucose trends at a glance."` — "trends" is accurate for interstitial data and preserves the headline's punch.

---

**Considered and not raised:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 (health impaired by non-use / improved by use). The copy is capability-framed, not fear-framed, and doesn't claim health improvement from use. Raising it here would be a false positive. § 11 nos. 8, 9, 11, 12 are not engaged by this asset. UWG § 6 is not engaged — no comparison.

## Paste-ready revision

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance.** Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Confirm with a fingerstick before dosing when your glucose is changing rapidly.

Same three-beat rhythm, same length. The third line now carries the limitation instead of contradicting it.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "every 5 minutes" | Measurement/display interval as specified in the technical file | Regulatory / R&D |
| "Real-time" | Sensor lag time and accuracy during rapid rate-of-change (MARD, rate-of-change stratified) | Clinical affairs |
| Any dosing-adjacent wording | Whether the CE certificate scope covers a non-adjunctive (dosing) indication — if it does, the intended purpose you supplied is not the one to review against | Regulatory / notified-body certificate |
| Limitation wording | The IFU's own phrasing of the rapid-change limitation, so the ad text tracks it | Regulatory |
| Market | Whether this runs in Germany — decides whether the HWG § 3 no. 2(a) and UWG § 5 exposure above is live | Marketing |

The third row is worth checking first. If the certificate covers non-adjunctive dosing, the "Dose with confidence" finding changes character entirely — it would become a substantiation question rather than an incurable (d) breach.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` **[verified]**
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` **[verified]** (conditional on DE market)
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7–9, 11, 12 — `references/hwg.md` **[verified]** — scoped, considered, not engaged
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` **[verified]** (conditional on DE market)

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

One thing I can't assess from what I have: whether CGM-specific dosing claims are constrained by guidance beyond the statute text. That turns on MDCG guidance and national enforcement practice, which this skill doesn't verify — point me at a source if you want it factored in, but I won't state a rule I can't cite from the reference files.

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`; also Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** (d) — the assessed intended purpose is *monitoring*, and it expressly states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change". (b) — it creates "a false impression regarding treatment" by presenting the reading as a sufficient basis to dose.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — **cannot be cured by evidence.** No accuracy data fixes this. It is cured only by narrowing the claim, or by extending the conformity assessment to a non-adjunctive dosing indication. If the device already holds such an indication, the intended purpose you supplied is not the one this copy is written against, and I'd need the correct text.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — "Erfolg mit Sicherheit", if DE market; "with confidence" is reassurance rather than an express guarantee, so this is arguable, not the strong point. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse", if DE market.
**Call:** **Cut**
**Suggested fix:** Delete. Replace with the confirmation instruction — see the full revised copy below.

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** "Real-time" ascribes a property the intended purpose itself contradicts. Interstitial glucose lags blood glucose — that lag is precisely what the rapid-change carve-out in your intended purpose describes. Presenting the reading as real-time tells the user it tracks their current blood glucose without delay.
**Evidence needed:** Lag characterisation from the clinical/performance data. Note this can support a *narrower* phrasing (e.g. a stated measurement interval), but no lag figure makes "real-time" accurate for a measurand that lags by design.
**Call:** **Reword**
**Suggested fix:** "Interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes" — drop "real-time", name the measurand.

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** Secondary to the above, and weaker standing alone — but "your glucose" without qualification presents an interstitial value as the user's glucose level, and "know" asserts certainty about a value the intended purpose says is not interchangeable with a blood measurement. Read in sequence with "Dose with confidence", it sets up the dosing implication rather than merely puffing.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — this is a wording fix, not a substantiation gap.
**Call:** **Reword**
**Suggested fix:** "Know your glucose trends at a glance." Trend framing is what a monitoring-only device actually delivers.

---

**Claim:** "every 5 minutes, straight to your phone"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A factual specification claim. Nothing in it conflicts with the intended purpose.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the 5-minute interval is the assessed sampling/display interval in the technical file, and that phone display is within the assessed system configuration (app is presumably part of the device or an accessory — if the app carries its own conformity scope, check the claim sits inside it). **Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "wesentliche Merkmale", if DE market and the interval or connectivity is stated more broadly than the technical file supports.
**Call:** **Verify**
**Suggested fix:** No change if the file confirms it.

**Asset-level finding — omission**
**Claim:** the copy as a whole
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:** The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. The limitation is not one I am inferring from the device category — **you supplied it**: readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change. **Call:** **Reword** — carry the limitation in the copy itself, not only in a footnote. Given this asset directs a dosing action, an IFU pointer alone is not proportionate here.

Three changes: trends not values; interstitial and no "real-time"; the dosing line inverted from a permission into the instruction the intended purpose requires. It keeps the original's rhythm and the "at a glance / to your phone" benefit framing.

That is limb (d), and limb (d) is fixed by narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment — not by data.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(d) prohibits "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out." Dosing is a treatment decision. The assessed purpose states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change." The copy suggests unqualified dosing off the device, with no rapid-change condition attached — a use the assessment did not cover.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Accuracy data during rapid excursion would not help; the limit is the scope of the assessment, not the performance.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` (Erfolg mit Sicherheit) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("Zwecktauglichkeit", "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") — if the German market is in scope. "Confidence" is not literally "certainty," so § 3 no. 2(a) is the weaker of the two; § 5(2) no. 1 is the direct mirror of the (d) breach and is the more likely Abmahnung hook.
**Call:** **Cut**
**Suggested fix:** `"Confirm with a fingerstick before dosing when your glucose is changing quickly."`

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have." Interstitial measurement lags blood glucose — that lag is the reason your own intended purpose carves out rapid-change treatment decisions. "Real-time" asserts a property the device does not have, and it asserts it in the exact dimension the assessed purpose disclaims.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the word "real-time." Substantiating lag characteristics would not make "real-time" accurate; it would show why it isn't.
**Call:** **Reword**
**Suggested fix:** `"Continuous readings"` or `"Readings every 5 minutes"` — drop "real-time" rather than qualify it.

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(b) prohibits "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis, functions or properties which the device does not have." "Your glucose" elides interstitial and blood glucose, and "at a glance" presents the number as sufficient on its own. Nothing in the sentence is a stated falsehood — which is precisely what limb (b) is for. The impression left is that the displayed value is the definitive glucose value, when the assessed purpose says it is not, in the situations that matter most clinically.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by wording, not data.
**Call:** **Reword**
**Suggested fix:** `"Know your glucose trends at a glance."` Adding "trends" does most of the work: it keeps the headline's rhythm and promise while moving the claim onto what a CGM actually delivers well.

---

**Claim:** "every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A narrow, verifiable performance figure of exactly the kind that is cheap to defend. Nothing in the intended purpose contradicts it.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the sampling/display interval in the technical documentation is 5 minutes and not, say, a 5-minute display of a 1-minute sample or vice versa. Also confirm it does not vary by app state or connection.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — only if the figure is wrong or conditional.
**Call:** **Verify**

---

### Asset-level: limb (c)

**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(c) is an omission test — "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose." The copy is benefit-only across all three sentences. The likely risk here is **named in the material you supplied**, not inferred by me from the device category: readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change. That is a risk arising from use exactly in line with the intended purpose, and the asset surfaces none of it.

This finding would be marginal on a 12-word banner, where an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix. It is not marginal here, because the copy does not merely omit the limitation — it affirmatively invites the use the limitation excludes.

**Call:** **Reword** — the fix is folded into the rewrite below.

## Paste-ready rewrite

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance.**
> Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone.
> Confirm with a fingerstick before dosing when your glucose is changing quickly.

Three sentences, same shape, same length, same promise structure. The third sentence now carries the (c) disclosure and neutralises the (d) breach in one move — instead of a bolted-on disclaimer, the limitation becomes the closing instruction.

If marketing pushes back on losing "Dose with confidence," the honest counter is that the phrase cannot be qualified into compliance. `"Dose with confidence — confirm with a fingerstick when glucose is changing quickly"` still leads with the excluded use. The suggestion is made by the headline; a trailing qualifier does not withdraw it.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "every 5 minutes" | Sampling and display interval as recorded in the technical documentation; whether it varies by app or connection state | Regulatory / R&D |
| Rapid-change wording | The IFU's own phrasing of the fingerstick-confirmation instruction — match the rewrite to it rather than paraphrasing | Regulatory |
| Audience | Whether this asset is gated to Fachkreise or public | Marketing |
| Market | Whether DE is in scope, which activates the HWG/UWG layer | Marketing |

## Open question I could not close

The IFU may record likely risks beyond the rapid-change limitation — insertion-site reaction, adhesive sensitivity, interfering substances are common in this device category. I have not flagged any of them, because I only have the intended purpose you pasted and a (c) finding built on an inferred risk is unfalsifiable. Worth a pass over the IFU's limitations and warnings section to see whether anything else belongs in patient-facing copy.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (contingent on DE market)
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` (contingent on DE market)

HWG § 11 was considered and **not** cited. For devices only nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 apply, and this copy carries no fear-of-non-use framing, no testimonial, no advertorial, and no under-14 targeting. UWG § 6 does not apply — there is no comparison.

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. ## Verdict

One must-fix, three should-fix. The copy isn't wholesale off-label — your intended purpose does permit treatment decisions — but it drops the exact condition the intended purpose was written to carve out. That gap is the problem.

## Findings

**1. "Dose with confidence" — must fix (unqualified where the intended purpose is conditional)**

Your intended purpose permits dosing *except* during rapid glucose change. The copy makes the permitted claim unconditionally, which means the promotional message is broader than the authorised purpose — the classic MDR Article 7 exposure (misleading as to intended purpose / ascribing performance the device doesn't have in all states). It also inverts the risk profile: rapid change is precisely when a user feels most urgency to dose and when the reading is least reliable.

Don't delete the benefit — condition it. E.g. "Dose from your sensor reading — fingerstick to confirm when glucose is changing fast." That keeps the commercial claim inside the label.

**2. "Real-time readings" — should fix**

"Real-time" asserts something the technology can't do, and it undercuts the rapid-change caveat by implying no lag. Interstitial glucose trails blood glucose; that lag *is* the mechanism behind your own limitation. Suggest "continuous," "live," or "updated every 5 minutes." (Separately: confirm 5 minutes is the actual display/update interval in the IFU and technical documentation, not the sampling rate — a mismatch is a performance-claim defect on its own.)

**3. "Know your glucose at a glance" — should fix**

Reads as blood glucose; the device measures interstitial glucose. "Your sensor glucose" or "your glucose trend" is accurate and costs nothing in punch. "At a glance" also implies alerting/notification — fine if the device has alarms in its intended purpose, misleading if it doesn't.

**4. Missing indication and limitation statement — should fix**

No population stated. As written, the copy addresses anyone with a phone, not "adults with diabetes"; wellness-adjacent framing on a diabetes-indicated Class IIa device invites an off-label-promotion finding. And there's no limitation text at all. Depending on channel, the "not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change" statement needs to appear with prominence comparable to the claims — not only in a footer. Add smartphone/OS compatibility and an IFU pointer.

## Suggested rewrite

> **Your glucose, continuously.**
> Sensor readings updated every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Dose from your sensor — confirm with a fingerstick when glucose is changing fast.
>
> For adults with diabetes. Sensor glucose readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change. Requires a compatible smartphone. Read the instructions for use.

## One thing to confirm

Whether the phone app is part of the CE-marked device. "Straight to your phone" is a functional claim; if the app is a separate or accessory component, or if a reader/receiver is also required, the copy needs to reflect that. Route the final version through regulatory affairs — I'm flagging claim-to-label consistency, not signing it off.

## Verdict

Don't ship as written. One line is a direct contradiction of the intended purpose, and two others need substantiation or softening.

## Findings

**1. "Dose with confidence" — blocking.**

This is the whole problem. In a diabetes context "dose" reads as insulin dosing, i.e. a treatment decision. Your intended purpose explicitly carves treatment decisions out during rapid glucose change, which means you do not hold a clean non-adjunctive indication. The copy therefore ascribes a function the device is not cleared for.

Under MDR Article 7 this is misleading on two counts: ascribing functions the device does not have (7(a)) and creating a false impression regarding treatment (7(c)). It's also off-label promotion — and it's the highest-harm failure mode in the whole ad, because a user who acts on it during a rapid excursion is dosing off a reading the manufacturer has already said is unreliable in exactly that scenario.

There is no wording fix that keeps the dosing meaning. Either cut it, or change the indication — and changing it means clinical evidence for non-adjunctive use plus notified body assessment, not a copy edit.

**2. "Know your glucose at a glance" — needs qualification.**

The device measures interstitial glucose; the copy says "your glucose", which a lay reader takes as blood glucose. Combined with removing the dosing line, this is survivable, but "your glucose levels and trends" or explicit "sensor glucose" is safer and costs you nothing.

**3. "Real-time readings every 5 minutes" — substantiate, and consider softening.**

Two separate issues. The 5-minute interval must match the IFU and technical documentation exactly — verify, don't assume. Separately, "real-time" sits awkwardly against interstitial lag (typically 5–15 min behind blood glucose). Claiming real-time knowledge of glucose overstates what the sensor delivers and quietly reinforces the dosing implication you just removed. "Updated every 5 minutes" carries the same benefit without the exposure.

**4. "Straight to your phone" — conditional.**

Fine if substantiated. Needs compatible-device/OS list, app requirement, and any connectivity or alarm caveats reachable from the ad. If alarms are a claimed feature elsewhere, the phone-dependency limitations need to travel with them.

**5. Missing mandatory content.**

No limitation statement, no IFU pointer. MDR 7(d) covers failure to inform of likely risk. At minimum, carry the intended-purpose limitation verbatim and a "read the instructions for use" line. Also check market-specific rules — Germany's HWG in particular imposes additional requirements on consumer-facing device advertising.

## Suggested rewrite

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance.**
> Sensor glucose readings updated every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. See where you're heading, not just where you are.
>
> *For continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes. Not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change. Read the instructions for use.*

"See where you're heading, not just where you are" is doing the work "Dose with confidence" was doing — it sells the genuine advantage of CGM over fingersticks (trend and direction) without touching therapy decisions.

If marketing pushes back on losing the dosing line, the honest answer is that the claim they want is an indication they don't have, and the route to it is clinical, not editorial.

One caveat: this is a copy review against the intended purpose you gave me, not regulatory sign-off. Route the final wording through regulatory affairs, and have them confirm the 5-minute interval against the current IFU.

"Class IIa" reads as EU MDR / UKCA framing, so I'm assessing against MDR Article 7 (claims) plus the general rule that promotional material can't exceed the intended purpose in the IFU. Adapt if this is actually a US 510(k)/iCGM asset — the dosing analysis is the same, the citation isn't.

---

## Line by line

**"Dose with confidence." — blocker, remove.**

Your intended purpose explicitly excludes replacing BG measurement for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change. "Dose" *is* the treatment decision. This is off-label promotion of a non-adjunctive indication the device doesn't hold, and it fails MDR Art. 7 on two counts at once: it creates the impression of a function the device doesn't have, and it omits a known risk — the exact scenario (rapid change, sensor lag) where acting on the reading can cause a dosing error and hypoglycaemia. It's also the line a regulator or a plaintiff would read first. There is no qualifying footnote that rescues it; the headline promise and the asterisk would contradict each other.

**"Know your glucose at a glance." — qualify.**

"Your glucose" reads as blood glucose to a lay audience; the device measures interstitial fluid. That conflation is the root of the dosing risk, so it isn't pedantry. "At a glance" is fine.

**"Real-time readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone." — conditionally OK.**

- "Real-time" is defensible *only* if this is genuinely rtCGM (automatic push) rather than intermittently-scanned. If it's isCGM, the word is a misrepresentation of a property.
- "Every 5 minutes" needs to match the IFU sampling interval exactly.
- "Straight to your phone" implies unconditional delivery. It depends on a compatible device, OS version, Bluetooth range, and app permissions — and if the app carries alarms, phone-dependency warnings are usually mandatory in the IFU and should not be contradicted in ads.

---

**Closest to your original, compliant:**

> Know your glucose trends at a glance. Continuous readings every 5 minutes, straight to your compatible phone. Manage your diabetes with more information.

**Stronger, leans into trend data — the thing the device is actually indicated for:**

> See where your glucose is heading. A new reading every 5 minutes, day and night, on your phone. Confirm with a fingerstick before you dose.

Putting the fingerstick line in the *body copy* rather than a footnote is the safer construction — it turns the limitation into a benefit statement ("we tell you when to check") instead of a disclaimer fighting the headline.

**If marketing insists on keeping a confidence note,** attach it to something true: "Spot highs and lows with confidence" — detection is in the intended purpose; dosing isn't.

---

- Population limit: adults with diabetes. Don't show a child, teen, or a visibly pregnant person in the creative.
- Rapid-change limitation stated somewhere legible, not 6pt.
- "Always read the instructions for use." CE mark with the Notified Body number (Class IIa with a measuring function / sterile route requires NB involvement).

# Device Claims Review: comparison block

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-09
**Device:** Class I software device (EUDAMED submission tool)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (as stated) — confirm gating if this is a public web page
**Markets:** DE (EU overlay applies)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 2 reword/substantiate, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed. All three sentences are comparative advertising under UWG § 6(1), and none currently clears § 6(2) no. 2.

The structural problem: the block is built entirely on comparison, and the comparisons are directed at unnamed competitors on characteristics the reader cannot check. Under § 6(2) no. 2 *nachprüfbar* is the sharp edge — a claim that is broad and unverifiable is expensive to defend even when it is true, and this is the classic Abmahnung shape.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Competitors leave you guessing."
**Breach:** UWG § 6(2) no. 5 [verified] — and § 6(2) no. 2 [verified]
**Why:** § 6(1) is engaged: read together with "legacy EUDAMED tools", competitors are *erkennbar* even though unnamed. The sentence then carries no objective content at all — it is not tied to any *wesentliche, relevante, nachprüfbare und typische Eigenschaft* (no. 2), and its only function is to characterise competitors' products as leaving users in the dark, which is the *herabsetzen* shape in no. 5.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. There is no data that makes a contentless disparagement objective.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** Delete. If the underlying point is error visibility, state it about your own product: "You see which fields fail validation, and why, before you submit."

---

**Claim:** "3x faster than the alternatives."
**Breach:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 [verified]; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified]
**Why:** § 6(2) no. 2 — a quantified comparison against unnamed "alternatives" with no stated task, method, baseline or date is not *nachprüfbar* by the reader from public information. § 5(2) no. 1 catches it independently as an *von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse* and *Tests* claim: a bare "3x" is a test-result claim whose essential components are withheld.
**Evidence needed:** A documented benchmark — what task was timed, which comparators, how many runs, when, by whom — and a published methodology the reader can reach.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified] — if the 3x figure is not supported for the device as it performs in line with its intended purpose, this ascribes a performance property it does not have. Whether speed of submission preparation is "performance" in the Art. 7 sense depends on the intended purpose I have not seen.
**Call:** Needs substantiation + rewording
**Suggested fix:** "In our [Month Year] benchmark, preparing a Class I registration took an average of [X] minutes in [Product] versus [Y] minutes entering the same data manually in the EUDAMED web interface. Methodology: [link]."
Note the comparator switch: benchmarking against manual entry in EUDAMED itself largely takes you out of § 6 — EUDAMED is not a *Mitbewerber* — while keeping the persuasive force. If you need a competitor comparison, name the product and version and publish the method.

---

**Claim:** "Unlike legacy EUDAMED tools, we validate every field before submission."
**Breach:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 [verified]
**Why:** The sentence makes two assertions. Yours ("we validate every field") is in principle verifiable from a demo or documentation. The implied negative ("legacy tools do not") is a comparison on a characteristic the reader cannot check from public information, which fails no. 2 regardless of accuracy. § 6(2) no. 1 is probably satisfied — EUDAMED submission tools serve the same *Bedarf* — so the comparison is not disqualified at the threshold; it fails on verifiability.
**Evidence needed:** For "every field": a list of the EUDAMED fields the tool validates and the ruleset used, confirming there is no carve-out (free-text, conditional, or actor-level fields that are not machine-checkable). "Every" is an absolute and has to be literally true. For the implied negative: documented, dated evidence of the named competitors' behaviour.
**Also engaged:**
- MDR Art. 7(a) [verified] — if any field class is not validated, "every field" ascribes a property the device does not have.
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) [verified] — *Erfolg mit Sicherheit*. Read with "competitors leave you guessing", the block edges toward promising that a validated submission will be accepted. This bites only if the copy is read as assuring the submission outcome rather than the field-level check; the fix below keeps the two apart. § 3 applies to Fachkreise, so the audience does not save it.
- MDR Art. 7(d) [verified] — cannot be assessed without the intended purpose. If the assessment covers field-level format checking but the copy is read as assuring regulatory compliance of the submission, that is intended-purpose drift.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "[Product] checks every EUDAMED data field against the current EUDAMED business rules before you submit, so format and completeness errors surface in your workspace instead of after submission."

---

### Limbs not engaged

- **Art. 7(b)** — no clinical impression. This is a regulatory data-submission tool; nothing in the copy suggests treatment or diagnosis.
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4** — the copy makes no claim about class, CE marking, notified-body involvement or certificate scope, so the status/*Zulassung* hook is not triggered by this text.
- **HWG § 11** — not applicable to Fachkreise. If this block sits on an ungated public page the audience analysis changes, but on these three sentences none of nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 would bite anyway.
- **HWG § 3a** — Arzneimittel only. Not applicable to devices.

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — for example, whether validation passing is documented as not guaranteeing acceptance, or whether any field class falls outside the check. Worth checking against the IFU. I am not raising (c) as a finding, because I cannot point to the risk in material you have supplied.

## Verdict

Three of the four sentences are not safely usable in Germany as written. The disparagement line is the highest risk; the "3x faster" line is the one most likely to draw an Abmahnung from a competitor.

---

## Issue by issue

**1. "Competitors leave you guessing." — Delete. No fix available.**

This is a blanket negative assertion about competitors' products with no factual comparison attached. That is textbook *Herabsetzung* under **§ 6(2) Nr. 5 UWG** (and § 4 Nr. 1 UWG independently). A comparison that disparages without comparing verifiable characteristics is unlawful regardless of whether it's true. In a market with few identifiable EUDAMED tool vendors, competitors are "erkennbar" even without naming them, so § 6 UWG applies. There's no wording that rescues the sentence — the claim itself is the defect.

**2. "3x faster than the alternatives." — Unusable without a named baseline and substantiation on file.**

Fails **§ 6(2) Nr. 2 UWG** (comparison must be of objectively verifiable, relevant, typical characteristics) and **§ 5 UWG**. "The alternatives" is undefined, "faster" doesn't say at what task, and there's no measurement method. Under German practice the burden of substantiation sits with you, and a superiority claim needs a demonstrable, non-transient lead. It also triggers **MDR Art. 7** (misleading claim as to performance) and, if the device is in HWG scope, **§ 3 HWG**.

Fix: compare against a *defined* baseline — ideally your own manual/spreadsheet workflow rather than competitor products, which keeps you out of § 6 UWG almost entirely — and state the task, the metric, the sample, and the date.

**3. "Unlike legacy EUDAMED tools" — Replace.**

"Legacy" is an unverifiable pejorative framing of an identifiable competitor group. Same § 6(2) exposure, weaker than #1 but not worth defending.

**4. "We validate every field before submission." — Two separate problems.**

- *Absolute claim:* if even one field is unvalidated (free text, conditional fields, attachments, fields the API doesn't expose), the claim is misleading under § 5 UWG / MDR Art. 7. Quantify instead.
- *Intended-purpose consistency:* MDR Art. 7 requires claims to stay within the intended purpose in your technical documentation and IFU. If the intended purpose is worded as "supports the user in preparing data," a validation claim overshoots it and becomes off-label promotion. Check the wording before the copy ships, not after.

Also avoid any phrasing implying the tool guarantees a compliant or accepted submission — that's an outcome you don't control, and it's the claim most likely to be read as misleading by a competent authority.

**Two things that do *not* constrain you here:** the audience is *Fachkreise*, so the § 11 HWG restrictions on advertising to the public don't apply. And as a Class I self-certified device you have no notified body — so no certification, approval, or endorsement language, and nothing suggesting the CE mark or EUDAMED itself implies Commission endorsement of your product.

---

## Rewritten copy

**English**

> Field-level validation against the EUDAMED data requirements — before you submit.
>
> [Product] checks [N] mandatory and conditional fields in the [Device] module against the current EUDAMED data dictionary and flags errors in your workspace, so you find them before the submission does.
>
> In internal testing ([month/year], n = [N] submissions), preparing a [Device] module submission took [Y] minutes with [Product] versus [Z] minutes preparing the same dataset manually in spreadsheets. Method and underlying data available on request.

**German**

> Feldgenaue Prüfung nach den EUDAMED-Datenanforderungen – vor der Übermittlung.
>
> [Produkt] prüft [N] Pflicht- und bedingte Felder des [Geräte-]Moduls gegen das aktuelle EUDAMED-Datenwörterbuch und markiert Fehler in Ihrer Arbeitsumgebung, bevor Sie übermitteln.
>
> In internen Tests ([Monat/Jahr], n = [N] Übermittlungen) dauerte die Vorbereitung einer Übermittlung im [Geräte-]Modul mit [Produkt] [Y] Minuten gegenüber [Z] Minuten bei manueller Aufbereitung in Tabellen. Methodik und Rohdaten auf Anfrage.

Have the German version reviewed against the English by someone who will catch claim inflation in translation — "prüft alle Felder" or "garantiert" creeping back in is a common way a cleaned-up claim gets un-cleaned.

- The field count [N] and which module/dictionary version it refers to, with a review trigger for when EUDAMED's dictionary changes — a claim that was accurate at launch goes misleading silently.

Realistic enforcement path is not the authority — it's a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale sending a cease-and-desist with a penalty clause and cost claim. That's why the substantiation file matters more than the wording.

The brief says Class I medical device, but the copy describes a EUDAMED regulatory-submission tool — data preparation for a registration database is not normally a medical purpose under MDR Art. 2(1). I've reviewed it as you specified, and the MDR Art. 7 points above assume the classification is correct. Worth confirming which product this copy actually belongs to, because a wrong classification claim in marketing is itself a misleading-advertising problem.

- **If it isn't:** only UWG applies. Still enough to make three of these four sentences actionable.

I've reviewed against both below. Your audience is `Fachkreise` (professionals), so the HWG §11 restrictions aimed at lay advertising don't bite — that's the one thing working in your favour.

## Clause-by-clause

**"Unlike legacy EUDAMED tools"** — Comparative advertising under UWG §6. "Legacy tools" reads as generic, but the EUDAMED tooling market is small enough that competitors are likely identifiable, which triggers the full §6(2) conditions: the comparison must be objective, verifiable, relevant, and representative. It also asserts a fact about competitor products (that they don't validate) which must be true of *every* product in the referenced class. One competitor with field validation makes this false.

**"we validate every field before submission"** — Absolute claim, must be literally true. EUDAMED contains conditional fields, free-text fields, and attachments where "validation" can only mean format/presence checking, not correctness. Under MDR Art. 7(a) this risks ascribing properties the device doesn't have. There's also a dangerous implied claim underneath it: that a validated submission will be accepted. Never imply a regulatory outcome.

**"Competitors leave you guessing"** — Cut this. It's disparagement (`Herabsetzung`) with no objective basis: UWG §4 Nr. 1, and §6(2) Nr. 5 in the comparative context. It compares nothing measurable, so it can't be defended by substantiating it — the only defence is deletion.

**"3x faster than the alternatives"** — Quantified superiority claim. Faster at what, measured how, against which alternatives, under what conditions, as of when? German courts routinely put the substantiation burden on the advertiser for superiority and comparative claims, and the claim must stay true as competitors ship updates — these go stale silently.

> Automated pre-submission validation for EUDAMED. Before you submit, we check [N] mandatory fields across the Actor, UDI-DI and Device registration modules for completeness and format errors, so you find problems at your desk rather than in a rejected submission.

> In our benchmark of [n] UDI-DI registrations completed in [month/year], teams using [Product] finished in an average of [X] minutes, compared with [Y] minutes preparing the same submissions manually. Methodology available on request.

Assemble before publication, not after the Abmahnung arrives:

- Exact field count and module scope backing the "[N] mandatory fields" figure, with the EUDAMED release version it was derived from
- Benchmark protocol: sample size, task definition, participant experience level, date, raw timings
- Named review owner and a re-verification date (EUDAMED module changes will invalidate the field count)
- German translation reviewed so qualifiers survive — "average," "in our benchmark," "mandatory fields" all need to land as precisely in German as in English

> "Every EUDAMED submission is checked against the current data dictionary before it leaves your desk — mandatory fields, formats and UDI-DI structure — so format rejections surface in your workspace, not in the Commission's response."

If you want to keep a speed claim, it needs to look like this:

> "In a benchmark conducted in [month/year], [n] regulatory professionals registered [specific task, e.g. 50 Basic UDI-DIs] in an average of [X] minutes using [product], compared with [Y] minutes using [named tool / described manual process]. Method, dataset and participant profile: [link]."

- Written benchmark protocol: task definition, comparator versions, dates, sample size, who ran it
- Mapping of each public claim to the intended purpose in the technical documentation (MDR Art. 7 traceability)

**There is no BGH leading case squarely on medical device efficacy substantiation.** If someone hands you one, be skeptical. The standard applied to devices is imported from the BGH's general health-advertising (HWG) case law, developed mostly on medicinal products and foods, and then applied to devices by the OLGs.

That's not a dodge — it's the practically useful point, because the imported standard is the *pharma* standard, which is the strict one.

**The doctrinal anchor** is the "gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis" line, whose canonical modern statement is *Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil* (BGH, 6.2.2013, I ZR 62/11 — docket from memory, verify). Paraphrasing the holding, not quoting it:

- An efficacy claim in health-related advertising is misleading under § 3 HWG unless it is covered by **gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis** at the time the advertising runs — not later.
- Where the claim rests on a study, the study must meet **recognised scientific standards**: as a rule randomised, controlled, blinded, adequately powered, and **published** in the professional literature so it can be scrutinised.
- If you cite a study that falls short of that, you may only do so while **disclosing its limitations**.

**The part that actually decides your case is the burden of proof.** In health advertising the BGH reverses the normal allocation: once a challenger shows the claim is scientifically contested, the *advertiser* must prove it is true. You would have to produce the substantiation, on the short timetable of a Verfügungsverfahren, and your n=12 unpublished in-house study would be the whole record.

Device-specific hooks sit alongside this: § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG brings Medizinprodukte inside the HWG, and **Art. 7 MDR** independently bans claims that mislead as to performance or attribute functions the device does not have — enforceable in Germany via § 3a UWG.

Three separate problems, any one of which is enough:

1. **n=12, unpublished, in-house.** This fails the standard on every axis at once — power, publication, independence. There is no reading of *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* it survives.
2. **No comparator.** Faster than what? Standard care? Gauze? A named competitor? An unstated baseline on a quantified superiority claim is independently misleading under § 5 UWG, and if a competitor is identifiable, § 6 UWG comparative-advertising rules stack on top. Quantified percentage claims draw the strictest scrutiny precisely because they sound precise.
3. **"Heals wounds" may exceed your intended purpose.** If your CE documentation declares something like moist wound management, an active healing-acceleration claim goes beyond the certified intended purpose and beyond what your clinical evaluation (Annex XIV) supports. That's an Art. 7 MDR / notified-body problem, not just an advertising one.

Enforcement risk here is not theoretical: the Verband Sozialer Wettbewerb and Wettbewerbszentrale work this exact niche, and an Abmahnung is cheap for them to send.

Drop the quantified claim. Your study can support internal decisions and a clinical-evaluation building block; it cannot support "40 %" in market-facing copy. Realistic paths, roughly in order of cost:

- Reframe to claims within your declared intended purpose and supported by the device's mechanism and existing literature (moist wound environment, exudate management, wear time, patient comfort) — these are defensible without a superiority RCT.

## The leading case

**BGH, Urteil vom 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649).

That is the anchor decision for substantiation of health-related efficacy claims, and it is the one German courts and Wettbewerbszentrale/competitor warning letters cite. Reaffirmed and refined in **BGH, Urteil vom 07.05.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – "Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation"** (claims addressed to Fachkreise are held to the same standard, not a laxer one).

## The standard it set

Four elements, all of which bite here:

**1. Gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis is the threshold.** A health-related efficacy claim is misleading (§ 3 HWG, § 5 UWG) unless it corresponds to secured scientific knowledge. "Plausible", "consistent with", or "supported by preliminary data" is not the test.

**2. Reversal of the burden of proof.** This is the practically decisive part. Normally a plaintiff proves misleadingness. In health-related advertising, once the claim is contested as scientifically unsecured, **the advertiser must plead and prove** that the claim is scientifically secured. You do not get to say "prove us wrong." Longstanding rule: whoever advertises with a scientifically disputed proposition without disclosing the counter-position assumes responsibility for its correctness.

**3. The evidence must exist at the time the advertising runs.** Substantiation acquired later does not cure an ad that was unsupported when published. (Corollary from the same line: a once-supported claim must be withdrawn if the science turns against it.)

**4. Study quality — the methodological floor.** Where you advertise *with a study*, the study must meet the recognised rules and principles of scientific research: as a rule **randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, with an adequate number of subjects, and published so as to have been exposed to scientific scrutiny (peer review)**. A study falling short of that cannot establish gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis. Basisinsulin also held that you may not advertise a result the study does not actually carry — e.g. a secondary or post-hoc endpoint presented as if it were the demonstrated effect.

## Applying it to your facts

Your n=12 unpublished in-house study fails on essentially every prong: not published (so never scrutinised), n=12 is not an adequate subject count for a quantified effect size, and in-house sponsorship without independent review compounds it. Under the burden-reversal rule you would be the party who has to prove "40% faster" in court, holding only that study. That is not a close call.

Two additional points, both specific to your device:

- **The device-specific softening, and its limits.** For medical devices where blinding or placebo control is methodologically impossible or unethical (common in wound care), courts accept evidence at the level recognised as standard *in that field* rather than mechanically demanding a double-blind RCT. That helps with study *design*; it does **not** relax adequate powering, publication/independent scrutiny, or the burden of proof. A 12-patient unpublished file benefits from none of it.
- **Art. 7 MDR is a second, independent hook.** Since 26 May 2021, HWG expressly covers medical devices (§ 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG), and Art. 7 MDR separately bans claims that mislead as to performance. Art. 7 is treated as a Marktverhaltensregelung under § 3a UWG, so a competitor can attack the claim on that basis too. Separately: "heals 40% faster" is a performance claim that must be covered by your clinical evaluation under Art. 61 MDR/Annex XIV — a claim your CER does not support is a regulatory exposure with your notified body, not only a UWG one.
- **The comparator is undefined.** "40% faster" than *what* — no dressing, standard gauze, a named competitor? An unspecified baseline is independently misleading, and if competitors are identifiable it pulls in § 6 UWG comparative-advertising requirements.

Realistically: either commission an adequately powered, published study fitting the accepted methodology for wound healing, or drop to a claim your dossier actually carries (moist wound environment, exudate management, etc. — function claims tied to the device's mode of action are a different and much easier evidentiary posture than a quantified healing-rate claim).

In health-related advertising the burden shifts: an advertiser who makes a claim implying scientific support **takes on the risk** that the claim is not scientifically established, and must itself prove substantiation once the opponent has substantiated that the scientific backing is absent or contested. The advertiser cannot benefit from an unresolved scientific dispute — an unsettled state of science defeats the claim rather than saving it.

On **study quality**, the same line of authority holds that a claim asserting scientific proof requires studies meeting recognised scientific standards — the reference point being randomised, placebo/comparator-controlled, blinded trials with an adequate number of subjects, published in peer-reviewed literature — and that a study **not designed and powered to test the advertised endpoint** cannot carry the claim (the post-hoc/subgroup problem; see also BGH, Urt. v. 07.05.2015 – I ZR 29/14). I'm less certain how much of the "peer-reviewed publication" requirement is BGH text versus OLG jurisprudence and the food/health-claims line — verify before quoting.

For devices specifically, the point worth confirming separately is that **CE marking and notified-body conformity assessment do not insulate an advertising claim from UWG/HWG review**. That is settled in practice and Art. 7 MDR makes it explicit. I have a case in mind (BGH, Urt. v. 07.04.2016 – I ZR 81/15 – "Repair-Kapseln") but not with enough confidence to hand you as authority.

## Applied to "Heals wounds 40% faster"

The copy does not survive this standard, on several independent grounds:

- **n=12, in-house, unpublished** is not *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* under any reading of the BGH line. It is not close.
- **No comparator.** 40% faster than what — gauze, no dressing, a named competitor, your own previous generation? A quantified comparative claim with an unstated reference is misleading under § 5 UWG on its own, and if a competitor is identifiable, § 6 UWG comparative-advertising rules attach as well.
- **You carry the burden**, in court, at your cost. A challenger only has to make the absence of secured science plausible; then it's your study on trial. An n=12 unpublished in-house study is the weakest possible position to be in when that shift lands.
- **Regulatory exposure separate from UWG.** A quantified healing-rate performance claim has to sit inside the CE-marked intended purpose and be supported by the clinical evaluation (Annex XIV). If "40% faster healing" isn't in your technical documentation and clinical evaluation, that's an Art. 7 MDR / MPDG problem with the competent authority, not just an unfair-competition problem.
- **A footnote won't cure it.** Disclosing "based on one small study" doesn't rescue a headline claim that lacks secured substantiation — the strictness attaches to the claim as the average addressee understands it.

On practical risk: the German market has unusually active private enforcement — Wettbewerbszentrale and the Verband Sozialer Wettbewerb, plus competitors. The realistic sequence is Abmahnung → demand for an Unterlassungserklärung with a Vertragsstrafe → einstweilige Verfügung within days if you don't fold, plus the cost of pulling and reprinting packaging and materials.

## What you can do instead

Claim only what the clinical evaluation actually supports, and drop the number. Substantiated property or mechanism claims (moisture-balance maintenance, autolytic debridement support, atraumatic removal, wear time) are defensible if they're in your technical documentation. If "faster healing" is commercially essential, it needs a properly designed, adequately powered, controlled and published trial with a defined comparator and a pre-specified healing endpoint — and the claim then has to be written to match that endpoint exactly.

Two things I'd want before you rely on any of this: get German regulatory/competition counsel to pull I ZR 62/11 and confirm the wording and the current state of the line as of 2026, and have them check whether a more recent BGH decision has addressed device claims squarely. If you can enable web search I can do the first-pass verification myself and come back with the checked citations.

# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy, continuous ECG patch

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-09
**Device:** Class IIa continuous ECG patch (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Fachkreise — cardiology trade press. HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does.
**Markets:** DE (EU-wide MDR Art. 7 applies regardless)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 must-reword, 2 substantiate, 1 OK.

This copy is disciplined. It tracks the intended purpose almost phrase-for-phrase, states the supervision condition rather than burying it, and — notably — declines to put a sensitivity/specificity figure in the ad. There are no breaches I can identify on the material supplied. What remains is two things to verify against the technical file and one cheap drafting improvement.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** "Single-lead ECG recording" is verbatim intended purpose. The 14-day figure is a performance/wear-time characteristic, not a use claim — it does not extend the indication, the population, or the setting, so limb (d) is not engaged. "Up to" is a ceiling, correctly hedged.
**Evidence needed:** Wear-time substantiation in the technical file — adhesive/skin-contact validation, battery and storage capacity, and signal quality maintained across the full 14 days. Confirm 14 days is the validated maximum and not a best-case bench figure.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*wesentliche Merkmale*, *Zwecktauglichkeit*) — if the validated wear time is shorter than 14 days, or if 14 days is achievable only under conditions the copy does not state.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** none needed if the file supports 14 days.

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is asserted, so there is no performance claim to overstate under Art. 7(a) or HWG § 3 no. 1. Offering data on request is a legitimate Fachkreise convention.
**Evidence needed:** Two things. (1) The on-request pack must actually exist and be releasable — and it becomes advertising in its own right the moment it is sent, so it is subject to the same Art. 7 and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("*Ergebnisse oder wesentliche Bestandteile von Tests*") test as the ad. Selective figures in that pack are where this claim would fail, not in the ad. (2) Confirm whose sensitivity and specificity these are: the device's detection algorithm, or the device-plus-clinical-review workflow. If the figures come from an analysis service or algorithm outside this device's conformity assessment, attributing them to the patch would engage Art. 7(a).
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — if the pack presents endpoints selectively, or reports performance for a rhythm subset while the copy speaks of "cardiac arrhythmias" generally.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** Consider naming the scope in the ad itself — e.g. "Sensitivity and specificity data (per-rhythm, [study name]) available on request." A narrow, verifiable claim is cheap to defend against an Abmahnung; a broad one is expensive even when true.

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Tracks the assessed intended purpose. It carries the supervision condition rather than dropping it, which is the usual limb (d) failure in this device category, and it says *detection*, not diagnosis, treatment, or outcome — so limb (b) is not engaged either. No guarantee of success (HWG § 3 no. 2(a)), no absence-of-side-effects claim (§ 3 no. 2(b)), no claim about the manufacturer (§ 3 no. 3(b)).
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

**Drafting note (not a finding): the population qualifier.**
The intended purpose is limited to **adults**; the copy is silent on population. Silence is not a suggestion of paediatric use, so I do not read this as an Art. 7(d) breach. But the qualifier costs two words and closes the gap entirely, and in a cardiology title where paediatric readers exist it is worth having.

### Paste-ready revised copy

> Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days. For use in adults under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request. See instructions for use.

The IFU pointer is the proportionate way to handle limb (c) in trade-press length — see the open question below.

## Open questions I cannot close from what you supplied

**Limb (c) — likely risk.** The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — for a 14-day adhesive patch, skin reaction and signal-quality/artefact limitations are the usual candidates, but I am not going to raise (c) on a risk I inferred from the device category rather than read in your material. Check the copy against the IFU's warnings and limitations section. If a likely risk is recorded there, the IFU pointer above is normally the proportionate fix at this length; patient-facing safety text is not expected in trade press.

**Language of publication.** The copy is in English but the market is Germany. HWG and UWG bite on the German rendering that actually runs. "Bis zu 14 Tage" must carry the same ceiling hedge as "up to 14 days" — if the German draft reads "14 Tage" flat, that is a different and weaker claim.

**Channel discipline.** Cardiology trade press is Fachkreise, so § 11 is out of scope here. If this same copy is repurposed onto an ungated web page, § 11 re-enters — and note that no. 9 (promotional purpose not clearly recognisable) applies to advertorial or native placements in trade press too, if that is the format you are buying.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated maximum wear time: adhesive, battery, storage, signal quality across full duration | Regulatory / R&D — technical documentation |
| "sensitivity and specificity data" | The on-request pack, checked for completeness and representativeness; confirmation the figures attach to this device's assessed scope | Clinical affairs |
| Limb (c) omission | IFU warnings/limitations section, compared against the copy | Regulatory |
| German rendering | Final German text with hedges intact | Marketing / translation |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1, no. 2(a), no. 2(b), no. 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) — scoping only, not applied (Fachkreise) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6 — considered, not engaged; the copy makes no comparison — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Publication call

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify. I can't clear it for publication — that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis.

**One-page brief for counsel:**

- **Asset:** ~30-word trade-press ad, Class IIa continuous ECG patch, cardiology trade press, Germany.
- **Claims cleared on the material supplied:** intended-purpose statement (tracks the assessed purpose verbatim, retains the supervision condition); "up to 14 days" as a hedged wear-time ceiling; "data available on request" as a non-assertive offer.
- **Provisions checked:** MDR Art. 7(a)–(d); HWG § 3; HWG § 11 held inapplicable on a Fachkreise finding; UWG § 5(2) no. 1; UWG § 6 not engaged.
- **Three things to ask counsel:**

  3. Does the on-request sensitivity/specificity pack need to meet the same standard as published advertising, and what should the release process look like?

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A recording-duration spec is a technical characteristic, not a use claim. It does not conflict with the operative words of any limb on the material supplied. **Evidence needed:** Validated wear time from the technical documentation — that "up to 14 days" is the assessed recording/wear duration (adhesive, battery, signal quality at day 14), not a best-case bench figure.
**Also engaged:**

Silence alone I do not read as a positive suggestion of another use, so this is not a breach as written.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*wesentliche Merkmale*) — if 14 days exceeds validated wear time.

**Call:** Needs rewording (add the population qualifier) + Verify (the 14-day figure)

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is stated, so there is no performance number to substantiate. The claim asserts only that such data exists and will be supplied. Nothing in it conflicts with Art. 7(a) as written.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm (1) the data exists in the technical file and can actually be released on request, and (2) **which arrhythmias it covers**.
**Also engaged:**

**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Tracks the assessed intended purpose almost verbatim, including the supervision condition. It states an indication (detection) without implying an outcome, a treatment benefit, or diagnostic conclusion by the device itself — so no Art. 7(b) impression problem, and no HWG § 3 no. 2(a) certainty framing.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

- **MDR Art. 7(b)** — no wellness framing, no reassurance language, no outcome implication. The copy says "detection", not "diagnosis" or "peace of mind".
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** (guaranteed success) — nothing promises certainty. Note that "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" is a *pointer* to data, not a success promise; if a later draft replaces it with something like "reliably detects", § 3 no. 2(a) and Art. 7(a) both come into play.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(b)** (no harmful effects) — no side-effect reassurance made.
- **HWG § 3 no. 3(b)** — no claims about the manufacturer's credentials or track record.

As written it has no "improve your heart health" framing, so no. 7 would likely still be clear — but in a sponsored trade-press placement, no. 9 (*Werbezweck nicht deutlich erkennbar*) turns on the publication's advertorial labelling, not on your text.

The copy surfaces no limitation or contraindication. It does partly discharge the (c) concern already, by stating on its face that use is under healthcare professional supervision — which signals that output requires clinical interpretation.

Beyond that I cannot tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in this asset. I am deliberately not inferring one from the device category. Worth checking against the IFU — and if it does record one, the proportionate fix for trade-press length is an IFU pointer, not patient-facing safety text.

## Suggested revision (paste-ready)

(3) Does omitting "in adults" from an otherwise purpose-tracking claim create exposure in your view, or is it immaterial for a Fachkreise audience?

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

## Verdict

The copy is close but not clean. Two issues I'd treat as blocking, two as should-fix. Nothing here is unfixable — it's mostly under-specification, not over-claiming.

(Regulatory-review perspective, not legal advice — get RA/legal sign-off before placement.)

---

## Blocking

**1. The population restriction "in adults" has been dropped.**
Your certified intended purpose is limited to adults. The copy is silent on population, which leaves it open to being read as covering paediatric use. That is squarely MDR Art. 7(d) — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out" — and, in the German forum, §14 MPDG plus §3 HWG (irreführende Werbung; HWG applies to medical devices via §1(1) No. 1a). Competitor `Abmahnung` risk under §§ 3, 5 UWG is realistic here; this is the kind of omission German competitors actually chase.

*Fix:* add "bei Erwachsenen" / "in adults". Non-negotiable.

**2. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" is a performance claim without a performance statement.**
This is the weakest line. It asserts that favourable diagnostic-accuracy data exist and invites the reader to infer they're good, while disclosing nothing that can be checked — no endpoint, no comparator, no population, no numbers. Problems:

- **§ 5a UWG** (withholding material information) and **§ 3 HWG** — an implied efficacy claim the reader cannot evaluate.
- **§ 6 HWG**: if you *do* then supply study material, references to expert opinions/publications must name the source precisely (author, publication, date, verbatim citation). Teasing data now and citing it sloppily later fails at the second step.
- Cardiology Fachkreise will read "on request" as "the numbers are unremarkable." It's commercially weak as well as legally exposed.

*Fix:* state the figures, or drop the sentence entirely. If you state them, you need: which arrhythmia (AF is not "arrhythmias" in general), reference standard (12-lead? simultaneous Holter? adjudicated review?), n, point estimates with 95% CI, and the source. Also specify whether the figures describe the **algorithm** or the **end-to-end system including HCP over-read** — these differ, and conflating them is itself misleading.

---

## Should fix

**3. "Up to 14 days" needs a tether to the IFU.**
Permissible if substantiated, but "up to" claims attract scrutiny under § 5 UWG when typical performance falls short. Confirm the 14 days is the validated maximum wear time in your IFU and is supported by battery life, adhesive/skin-contact biocompatibility, and signal-quality data over the full duration — not a best-case bench figure. Add "maximale Tragedauer gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung."

**4. No risk signposting / IFU reference.**
MDR Art. 7(c) prohibits "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device." A 14-day adhesive wear claim with zero reference to the IFU is thin. A standard "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten" line, plus CE/class identification, closes this cheaply. Not a formal Pflichtangaben requirement — § 4 HWG covers medicinal products, not devices — but it's the industry norm and it neutralises the Art. 7(c) argument.

---

## Two things to check on your side

**"Continuous" must not imply real-time alerting.** If this is a store-and-forward patch analysed after return, ensure surrounding creative (headline, imagery, "continuous monitoring" phrasing) doesn't suggest live monitoring or alarms. The body copy correctly says "recording" — keep it that way.

**Fachkreise gating must be real.** The § 11 HWG restrictions on Publikumswerbung don't apply here, but only as long as placement stays inside the trade channel. If this copy is reused on an ungated website or in patient-facing material, re-review it — testimonials, case histories and technical/expert framing all become problematic.

**Language:** final placement must be German. Have the translation reviewed against the certified intended purpose wording — claim drift in translation is common, especially "Erkennung" vs. "Diagnose." Do not let it become "Diagnose."

---

## Suggested revision

**German (for placement):**

> **[Produktname]** – einkanaliges (Single-Lead) EKG-Aufzeichnungssystem
> Kontinuierliche EKG-Aufzeichnung **bei Erwachsenen** über eine Tragedauer von **bis zu 14 Tagen** (maximale Tragedauer gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung). Zur Anwendung **unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal** zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen.
> Sensitivität **XX %** (95 %-KI XX–XX), Spezifität **XX %** (95 %-KI XX–XX) für die Erkennung von [Vorhofflimmern] gegenüber [Referenzstandard]; [Autor et al., Publikation, Jahr; n = XXX].
> CE-gekennzeichnet, Klasse IIa. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung.
> *Information für Fachkreise.*

**English (for internal sign-off):**

> Single-lead ECG recording **in adults**, continuous, for wear durations of up to 14 days (maximum wear time per IFU). For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity XX % (95 % CI XX–XX), specificity XX % (95 % CI XX–XX) for detection of [AF] versus [reference standard]; [citation, n = XXX]. CE-marked, Class IIa. Consult the instructions for use.

---

## What I need from you to finalise

1. Does the IFU state 14 days as the validated maximum wear time?
2. The actual sensitivity/specificity figures — with endpoint, comparator, n, and citation. If these don't exist in citable form yet, cut the line rather than reword it.
3. Algorithm-only or system-level (including HCP over-read) performance?
4. Is analysis retrospective (store-and-forward) or does the product offer any real-time function?

Answer 1–4 and I'll produce the final German copy with the numbers dropped in.
